summary:
OUTPOST is a free browser game for children aged 7 to 12 in which they run a small crew on the Moon or Mars for 14 days. Every day the solar panels make a few blocks of power, and there is never enough for everything: life support, the greenhouse, radiation shielding and science research all compete. Players learn the trade-off real mission planners face: keep the crew alive, protect them from radiation, and still do the science that justifies the trip.
The solar storms are real flares from NASA's DONKI space weather database, and the background radiation comes from measurements by Curiosity's RAD instrument on Mars and Chang'E-4 on the Moon. Air leaks, marsquakes and dust devils are taken from real missions, and each one tells the player where it really happened.
A spoken three-day training mission with Comet, the crew's dog, points at every button, so a child who has never played can start alone. The whole game, voice included, works in English and in Arabic, written right to left, so Arab children can see themselves exploring space in their own language. It runs in any modern browser, with nothing to install.
details:
What it does

OUTPOST is a strategy game for children aged 7 to 12. The player commands a two-person crew at a base on the Moon (the rim of Shackleton crater) or on Mars (Jezero crater) for 14 days. Each day the solar panels make a handful of power blocks, and the player shares them between four systems: Life Support (air), Greenhouse (food), Shielding (a robot piles soil on the habitat to block radiation) and Science Research (the rover and the lab, which is the score). There is never enough power for all four, so every day is a choice. That is the real problem mission planners face.

How it works

•     14 days in 4 levels. Level 1 builds the base one system at a time. Each later level gives one block less power, and the solar storms get bigger.

•     The solar storms are real flares from NASA's DONKI database, in the order they happened. The game first asks DONKI for the latest flares; when it cannot get them, it plays stored DONKI records from the May 2024 Gannon storm. A badge always says which one you are playing.

•     On a storm day the player sees, before choosing, how much radiation the crew will take if they keep working and if they shelter. The shield is a blue dome that cracks, turns red and breaks, and keeps its scars.

•     Background radiation comes from measured values: Curiosity's RAD instrument on Mars and Chang'E-4's LND instrument on the Moon.

•     On quiet days, events change the plan: an air leak, mould in the greenhouse, a moonquake or marsquake, a lucky find, a dust devil. Each one says where it really happened, such as the air leaks on the International Space Station or the marsquakes recorded by InSight.

•     After each level a supply rocket brings three upgrades, and the player keeps one.

•     Pressing Run plays the day out in an animated picture of the base: the fan spins, the plants grow, and the rover drives out with Comet the dog.

•     At the end the crew flies home. The player gets a score (science + crew health + 5 points per day survived), their best score so far, how far they got, and up to three tips on what to change next time, based on what went wrong in that game.

Learning without a manual

A three-day training mission teaches the game. Comet, the crew's dog, says every instruction out loud, points at the exact button with an arrow, and waits until the player does it: air first, then food, then science, then shelter from a real X-class flare. A child who cannot read the meters yet can still follow the dog.

For Arab children: dream big

The whole game works in Arabic as well as English: every word, a right-to-left layout, an Arabic font, and Comet speaking Arabic. A child can learn in the language they think in. The title screen carries the flags of Egypt and Sudan. The Arab world is already in space: the UAE's Hope probe has orbited Mars since 2021, Sultan AlNeyadi became the first Arab to walk in space in 2023, and Rayyanah Barnawi became the first Arab woman in space the same year. OUTPOST wants an Arab child playing in Arabic to think: that could be me.

Benefits and intended impact

•     It teaches trade-offs and systems thinking, not just facts: you cannot have everything, so you decide what matters most today.

•     It shows how real space science works, with real NASA data, and it clearly separates what is measured from what is simplified.

•     It is free, with no account, no ads and no personal data collected. Saves stay on the player's own device.

•     It runs in any modern browser on a phone, tablet or school computer, and works offline after the first visit.

•     It fits a lesson: training takes a few minutes and a full mission about 10 minutes.

Tools and languages

JavaScript, HTML, CSS and SVG, with no frameworks, no build step and no server. The Web Audio API plays the music and sound effects, the Web Speech API speaks the guide, a service worker makes it work offline, and the browser's local storage keeps saves and best scores. The game asks NASA's DONKI service for flares straight from the player's browser. 92 automated tests check the game rules (Node.js), and complete games were played automatically in Google Chrome (Playwright) in both languages, on desktop and phone screen sizes. Fonts: Archivo, JetBrains Mono and Readex Pro (SIL Open Font License).

What makes it creative

•     The choice is the lesson. The game never gives the right answer; it shows what each choice will cost before you make it.

•     Real flares in their real order. In the stored May 2024 records, the Sun builds from M-class flares to an X8.7, as it really did.

•     Radiation you can see. It is invisible in real life, so the game turns it into a shield dome that cracks.

•     A dog as the teacher. Comet notices trouble first, barks, and tells you how each day went.

•     Honest by design. A “What is not real” section lists every simplification the game makes.

What we considered

•     Accuracy: measured values are labelled as measured, and game rules as rules. Turning a flare class into a surface dose is a simplification, and the game says so.

•     Reading level: short sentences, few numbers on screen, colours and pictures that carry the meaning, and a voice that reads instructions aloud.

•     Accessibility: keyboard play, screen-reader announcements and large buttons.

•     Difficulty: the mission starts easy and gets harder, and automated tests check that it can be won and that neither extreme (all safety or all science) wins.

•     Slow internet: the game is small, and if NASA's servers cannot be reached it still plays from stored real data.

Play it: https://nylocalsajid.github.io/Outpost/
